That is why we standardised on 6, then 8, and I upgraded services to .NET 10.|Benefits: cross-platform containers on Linux, better performance, built-in DI, minimal APIs, side-by-side runtimes.
p1-1.qa: .NET Framework is the original Windows-only runtime (last version 4.8.1, maintenance only). .NET Core was the cross-platform, open-source rewrite, and from .NET 5 it is simply ".NET": even-numbered releases (.NET 6, 8, 10) are LTS with 3 years of support, odd ones are STS with 2 years (since .NET 9).
i: Runtime model: .NET Framework is installed machine-wide and tied to Windows and IIS; modern .NET can be self-contained per app, runs on Linux containers and is side-by-side versioned.
Missing in modern .NET: WCF server (use CoreWCF or gRPC), Web Forms, AppDomains, .NET Remoting; that is why migrations need redesign in places.
Performance: every release brings big runtime and JIT wins (tiered compilation, Dynamic PGO on by default in .NET 8, faster GC); upgrading is often the cheapest performance fix.
Support dates: .NET 8 support ends November 2026, .NET 10 (November 2025) is supported until November 2028; in a GxP product staying on a supported runtime is a compliance requirement.
My experience: SharePoint and .NET Framework at DXC, ASP.NET Core on .NET 6 and 8 at IQVIA, and I upgraded [3] IRT services to .NET 10.

f: What is .NET Standard?
A shared API contract for libraries targeting both .NET Framework and .NET Core; for new libraries target net8.0 or net10.0 directly.
LTS vs STS?
LTS gets 3 years of support, STS 2 years (from .NET 9); regulated products stick to LTS.

p1-2.a: Value types (int, bool, struct, enum) hold the data itself and are copied on assignment.|Reference types (class, string, array, delegate) hold a reference to an object on the managed heap; assignment copies the reference.|Value types usually live inline (stack or inside their containing object); boxing wraps a value type into an object on the heap, which costs an allocation.|Use structs for small, immutable data; classes for identity and behaviour.
p1-2.qa: Value types (struct, enum, int, DateTime) hold their data directly and are copied on assignment; reference types (class, string, arrays, delegates) hold a reference to an object on the managed heap, so copies share the same object. Where they live depends on context: locals of value type usually sit on the stack, but a value-type field of a class lives inside that object on the heap.
i: Boxing: converting a value type to object or an interface allocates a heap copy; avoid in hot paths (non-generic collections, string.Format with ints in old code).

Equality: value types compare field by field (ValueType.Equals uses reflection unless overridden, so implement IEquatable<T>); reference types compare identity unless overridden; records give value equality for classes.
Nullability: value types need Nullable<T> (int?) to be null; reference types can be null, and nullable reference types (C# 8) warn you at compile time.
Passing: both are passed by value by default, but for a reference type the reference is copied, so the method can mutate the same object; ref/out/in pass by reference.
Guideline: make structs small (16 bytes or so) and immutable (readonly struct), otherwise copies cost more than allocations.
f: Is string a value type?
No, it is a reference type with value-like behaviour: immutable and compared by value with ==.
Are value types always on the stack?
No; that is a common myth. They live wherever their container lives, e.g. inside a class on the heap.

p1-3.a: The compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine; at each `await` on an incomplete Task it registers a continuation and returns the thread to the pool.|No new thread is created for I/O; the thread is freed while the database, HTTP call or file read is in flight, so a server handles more requests with fewer threads.|When the I/O completes, the continuation resumes (in ASP.NET Core there is no SynchronizationContext, so `ConfigureAwait(false)` matters mostly in libraries).|Rules: async all the way, never `.Result` or `.Wait()` (deadlocks, thread starvation), avoid `async void` except event handlers, pass CancellationToken.

messages.note: No thread is blocked while I/O runs

p1-3.qa: The compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine. At each await on an unfinished task it saves the method's state, returns an incomplete Task to the caller and frees the thread; when the awaited operation completes, a continuation resumes the method from where it stopped, possibly on another thread.
i: Nothing is "running" during I/O: an async database or HTTP call holds no thread while waiting; that is why async scales ASP.NET Core under load.
The awaiter pattern: await works on anything with GetAwaiter() (IsCompleted, OnCompleted, GetResult); if the task already completed, execution continues synchronously without a context switch.
Context: in UI apps the continuation returns to the captured SynchronizationContext; ASP.NET Core has none, so ConfigureAwait(false) matters mainly in libraries.
Exceptions are stored in the Task and re-thrown at await; async void methods cannot be awaited and crash the process on exceptions, so only use them for event handlers.
Pitfalls: .Result or .Wait() (sync-over-async) blocks a thread and can deadlock with a context; CPU-bound work does not become faster with async, use Task.Run only to offload from a UI thread.
In IRT every API call to SQL Server, SFTP and RabbitMQ is async with CancellationToken from HttpContext.RequestAborted, so abandoned requests stop work early.
f: Does async make code faster?
Not a single request; it improves throughput and scalability because threads are not blocked during I/O.
What does the state machine contain?
The method's locals, the current state number and the awaiters, stored in a struct that is boxed to the heap only if the method actually suspends.

p1-4.a: A Thread is an OS-level worker; expensive to create and you manage it yourself.|A Task is a promise of future work, scheduled on the thread pool or representing pure I/O with no thread at all.|ValueTask avoids a heap allocation when the result is often available synchronously (for example a cache hit); it must be awaited only once.|In web APIs I use Task by default and ValueTask only in hot paths after measuring.
p1-4.qa: A Thread is an OS thread you manage directly; a Task is a promise of a future result that usually runs on thread-pool threads or represents pure I/O with no thread at all. ValueTask<T> is a struct alternative to Task<T> that avoids an allocation when the result is often available synchronously.
i: Prefer Task for almost everything; create raw threads only for special long-running, dedicated work (or use TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning).
Task.Run queues CPU work to the thread pool; never use it to "make" I/O async in ASP.NET Core, it just burns a pool thread.

ValueTask rules: await it only once, never await it concurrently, never call .Result before it completes; convert with .AsTask() if you need more. Use it for hot paths that are usually synchronous (cache hits).
Task.WhenAll for parallel independent I/O; Parallel.ForEachAsync (.NET 6) for bounded parallel loops with MaxDegreeOfParallelism.
Thread-pool starvation shows as rising latency with low CPU; causes are sync-over-async and blocking calls.
c:
public ValueTask<StudyConfig> GetConfigAsync(Guid id) =>
    _cache.TryGetValue(id, out StudyConfig? c) ? ValueTask.FromResult(c!) : new(LoadAndCacheAsync(id));
f: When would you use a dedicated Thread?
Rarely: e.g. a long-running loop that must not occupy a pool thread, or code needing a specific apartment state; BackgroundService covers most cases.
Task.WhenAll vs awaiting in a loop?
WhenAll starts all operations together and waits once; a loop awaits them one by one.

p1-5.a: IEnumerable<T> iterates in memory; LINQ operators run as C# delegates on the client.|IQueryable<T> builds an expression tree that a provider (EF Core) translates to SQL, so filters run in the database.|List<T> is a materialised, in-memory collection with indexing and Count.|Classic bug: calling `.ToList()` or casting to IEnumerable too early pulls the whole table into memory before filtering.
p1-5.qa: IEnumerable<T> is an in-memory, forward-only sequence evaluated with LINQ-to-Objects in your process; IQueryable<T> holds an expression tree that a provider such as EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database; List<T> is a concrete, materialised collection already in memory.
i: The crucial difference: filtering an IQueryable adds a WHERE to SQL, while filtering after converting to IEnumerable (AsEnumerable or ToList) pulls every row into memory first.
IQueryable methods take Expression<Func<T,bool>>; IEnumerable methods take Func<T,bool> delegates, so custom C# methods work there but not in SQL.
Return types: repositories returning IQueryable leak query logic to callers; returning IEnumerable from a materialised list hides the cost; returning IReadOnlyList<T> is explicit.
Multiple enumeration: an IEnumerable from a query or yield runs again each time you enumerate it; materialise once with ToList when you need it twice.
In IRT the shipment list query stays IQueryable until paging and projection, so SQL Server returns only [50] rows of the DTO columns.
c:
IQueryable<Shipment> q = _db.Shipments.Where(s => s.StudyId == id);   // nothing executed yet
var page = await q.OrderBy(s => s.ShipmentDate).Skip(0).Take(50)
                  .Select(s => new ShipmentRow(s.Id, s.Status)).ToListAsync(ct); // one SQL query
var bad = _db.Shipments.AsEnumerable().Where(s => s.StudyId == id);   // loads the whole table!
f: What is an expression tree?
Code represented as data (Expression<T>) that a provider can inspect and translate, e.g. into SQL.
IEnumerable vs ICollection vs IList?
IEnumerable only iterates; ICollection adds Count/Add/Remove; IList adds index access.

p1-6.a: An interface is a contract: what a type can do; a class can implement many. Since C# 8 interfaces may have default implementations.|An abstract class is a partial base: it can hold state, constructors and shared logic; single inheritance only.|Use an interface for capabilities and for DI/mocking (for example ISftpClient); use an abstract class when providers share real code.|In my SFTP component the common abstraction is an interface, with a base class holding shared retry and logging logic.
p1-6.qa: An abstract class is a partially implemented base type that can hold state, constructors and shared code, and a class can inherit only one; an interface is a contract that a class or struct can implement many of. Since C# 8 interfaces can have default implementations and static members, but still no instance fields or constructors.
i: Use an interface for capabilities and seams for DI and testing (ISftpClient, IClock); use an abstract class to share real code and enforce a template (SftpClientBase with retry and logging).
Template Method pattern: the abstract base defines the algorithm and calls abstract or virtual steps; that is how our SFTP base class wraps every provider call with retry, logging and error mapping.
Versioning: adding a member to an interface breaks implementers unless it has a default implementation; adding a virtual method to a base class does not.
Combine them: interface for consumers, abstract base for implementers (ISftpClient + SftpClientBase).
Static abstract interface members (C# 11) enable generic math and factory patterns.
f: Can an abstract class implement an interface?
Yes, and it may leave members abstract for subclasses to implement.
When do default interface methods make sense?
Evolving a public interface without breaking existing implementers.

p1-7.a: S: one reason to change; for example a CSV parser separate from the validator and the importer.|O: open for extension, closed for modification; adding Rebex as a new SFTP provider meant a new class, not editing callers.|L: any ISftpClient implementation (ComponentPro, SSH.NET, Rebex) can replace another without breaking the caller.|I: small interfaces; readers do not depend on write methods.|D: high-level services depend on abstractions injected through ASP.NET Core DI.

p1-7.qa: SOLID is five design principles that keep code easy to change: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation and Dependency inversion. I can show each one in my SFTP integration and CSV import work.
i: S: the CSV import is split into parser, validator and importer classes, so a new validation rule never touches parsing code and each piece has focused unit tests.
O: adding Rebex meant one new ISftpClient class plus configuration; no caller or switch statement changed.

L: every provider honours the same contract (same exceptions mapped to SftpException, same behaviour on missing files), so swapping one for another cannot break callers; violating it would be a provider that silently ignores overwrite flags.
I: reporting code depends on a small IShipmentReader, not a large repository with write methods, so read services cannot write by accident.
D: high-level services depend on abstractions registered in ASP.NET Core DI; tests inject fakes and Moq mocks.
Balance: SOLID is a tool, not a goal; I avoid interfaces with exactly one implementation unless they are a test seam or a boundary.
f: Which principle is broken most often?
Single responsibility: services grow into god classes; I split by reason to change.
What is the difference between DI and DIP?
DIP is the design principle (depend on abstractions); DI is the technique that supplies those abstractions at runtime.

p1-8.a: Strategy/Adapter: SFTP providers behind one interface, selected by configuration.|Factory: creating the right provider or handler at runtime.|Repository and Unit of Work over EF Core for data access in some services.|Decorator: adding retry/logging around a client without changing it.|Options pattern and Singleton (via DI) for configuration and shared clients; Observer/pub-sub through Kafka and RabbitMQ.

rows: Create the right type at runtime

p1-8.qa: In production I have used Strategy and Adapter (SFTP providers behind one interface), Factory (choosing a provider by configuration), Decorator (adding retry and logging around clients), Repository/Unit of Work over EF Core in some services, Options and Singleton through DI, Observer/pub-sub via Kafka and RabbitMQ, plus Outbox and Retry for messaging.
i: Strategy: the algorithm (SFTP provider) is chosen at runtime; Adapter: each provider wraps a third-party API (Rebex, SSH.NET) into our ISftpClient.
Factory: SftpClientFactory reads the vendor's configured provider; with .NET 8 keyed services this is a one-liner.
Decorator: wrap an interface to add behaviour without changing it, e.g. a caching or retry decorator registered with Scrutor's Decorate.
Mediator (MediatR) and CQRS: separate commands and queries in larger services; useful but I avoid it in small ones to keep code simple.
Outbox: save the business change and the event in one transaction, then publish, so events are never lost when the broker is down.
I name patterns only when they clarify intent; the goal is simpler code, not pattern count.
f: Strategy vs Factory?
Strategy is the interchangeable behaviour; the factory decides which strategy instance to create.
A pattern you regret using?
Generic repositories on top of EF Core: they hid useful EF features and added code without value.

p1-9.a: The GC is generational: new objects go to Gen 0; survivors are promoted to Gen 1, then Gen 2. Most objects die young, so Gen 0 collections are cheap and frequent.|Objects over 85 KB go to the Large Object Heap, collected with Gen 2.|The GC frees managed memory only; unmanaged resources (files, sockets, DB connections, SFTP sessions) need IDisposable and `using`.|Server GC is the default for ASP.NET Core; watch for leaks from static caches, event handlers never unsubscribed, and captured closures.
p1-9.qa: .NET uses a generational, compacting, tracing garbage collector: it finds objects no longer reachable from roots (statics, stack, registers, handles), frees them and compacts the heap. New objects go into generation 0, survivors are promoted to 1 and 2, and large objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the Large Object Heap.
i: Generations work because most objects die young; gen 0 collections are cheap, gen 2 (full) collections are expensive.
Server GC (default in ASP.NET Core) uses a heap and GC thread per core for throughput; workstation GC suits desktop; concurrent/background GC reduces pauses.
LOH is not compacted by default, so repeated large allocations fragment memory; rent buffers from ArrayPool<T> instead.
Containers: the GC respects container memory limits; .NET 8 adds DATAS (dynamic adaptation of server GC heaps, default in .NET 9) for lower memory in small containers.
Finalizers delay collection by a cycle; implement IDisposable for deterministic cleanup and use SafeHandle instead of finalizers.
Diagnose with dotnet-counters (gc-heap-size, gen-2 count, % time in GC) and dotnet-gcdump; I used them for [a memory growth issue caused by an unbounded static cache].
f: What causes memory leaks in .NET?
Objects kept reachable: static collections, event handlers not unsubscribed, caches without limits, captured closures.
Should you call GC.Collect()?
Almost never; it disrupts the GC's tuning. Fix the allocation pattern instead.

p1-10.a: A delegate is a type-safe function pointer.|Func<T, TResult> returns a value; Action<T> returns void; Predicate<T> returns bool.|An event is a delegate with restricted access: only the owner can raise it, others can subscribe or unsubscribe.|Lambdas are inline anonymous functions; they can capture variables (closures), which is powerful but can extend object lifetimes.
p1-10.qa: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method; Func<> and Action<> are built-in generic delegates (Func returns a value, Action returns void); a lambda is concise syntax for creating a delegate or an expression tree; an event is a delegate wrapped so outsiders can only subscribe (+=) and unsubscribe (-=), not invoke or overwrite it.
i: Multicast: delegates can hold several methods; invoking runs them in order, and only the last return value is kept.
Closures: lambdas capture variables, not values; capturing a loop variable or a large object can surprise you or keep it alive longer.
Lambdas become Expression<Func<...>> when the target type asks for it; that is how EF Core reads your Where clause.
Event pattern: EventHandler<TEventArgs>, raise with `Handler?.Invoke(this, args)`; unsubscribe to avoid leaks when the publisher outlives the subscriber.
In ASP.NET Core, middleware is literally a chain of RequestDelegate instances, and Polly policies take Func<CancellationToken, Task> delegates.
f: Why use events instead of public delegates?
Events stop outside code from invoking the delegate or replacing all subscribers with =.
Func vs Predicate?
Predicate<T> is an older delegate equal to Func<T,bool>; LINQ uses Func.

p1-11.a: Most LINQ operators (Where, Select) do not run until you enumerate (foreach, ToList, Count, First).|Each enumeration re-runs the query, so enumerating an IQueryable twice means two database round trips.|Materialise once with ToList/ToArray when you need the results repeatedly.|Immediate operators: ToList, ToDictionary, Count, Sum, First, Any.
p1-11.qa: LINQ queries are not executed when you write them, only when you enumerate them (foreach, ToList, Count, First). The query is a recipe; each enumeration runs it again against the current data.
i: Deferred operators: Where, Select, OrderBy, Skip, Take; immediate operators: ToList, ToArray, Count, Sum, First, Any.
For IQueryable the whole chain is translated to one SQL statement at enumeration, so you can compose filters conditionally before executing.
Multiple enumeration pitfall: enumerating twice runs the database query or the yield iterator twice; analyzers warn about it.
Captured variables are read at execution time, not when the query was defined.
Exceptions inside the query appear at enumeration time, which can be far from the line that built it.
I use this for dynamic filters in IRT list endpoints: add Where clauses only for the parameters the user supplied, then page and execute once.
f: How do you force execution?
Call ToList/ToArray (or an aggregate) to materialise the results once.
Is deferred execution good or bad?
Good for composition and efficiency; risky when it causes repeated or late execution.

p1-12.a: Prefer immutability and avoiding shared state.|`lock` for short critical sections; `SemaphoreSlim` for async code (lock cannot contain an await) or to limit concurrency, for example parallel node deployments.|Concurrent collections (ConcurrentDictionary, Channel<T>) and `Interlocked` for counters.|Avoid double-checked locking bugs by using Lazy<T>; be careful with singletons that hold mutable state.
p1-12.qa: Code is thread-safe when concurrent callers cannot corrupt shared state. The best way is to avoid shared mutable state (immutability, local variables, scoped services); when sharing is needed, use the right primitive: lock, SemaphoreSlim for async code, Interlocked for counters, and concurrent collections.
i: lock (Monitor) for short synchronous critical sections; you cannot await inside a lock, so use SemaphoreSlim(1,1) with WaitAsync for async sections.
Interlocked.Increment and CompareExchange for lock-free counters and flags.
ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd can run the factory more than once; wrap the value in Lazy<T> if the factory must run exactly once.
Immutable records and ImmutableArray make sharing safe by design; .NET 8 adds FrozenDictionary for fast read-only lookups.
DI: singletons are shared by all requests, so they must be thread-safe; DbContext is not thread-safe, so never share it across concurrent tasks.
Across instances (several ECS tasks) in-process locks do nothing; use database locks, optimistic concurrency or a distributed lock. Our study transfer guard uses a lock row inside a transaction.
f: lock vs Monitor vs Mutex?
lock is syntax for Monitor (in-process, fast); Mutex can be cross-process and is slower. .NET 9 adds System.Threading.Lock as a dedicated lock type.
What is a race condition?
The result depends on timing between threads, e.g. two requests reading and writing the same counter.

p1-13.a: class: reference type with identity; equality by reference.|record (class): reference type with value-based equality, `with` expressions and concise immutable syntax; good for DTOs and events.|struct: value type, copied on assignment; `record struct` adds value equality.|I use records for API contracts and messages published to Kafka or RabbitMQ.
p1-13.qa: A class is a reference type with identity; a struct is a value type copied by value; a record is a type (record class by default, or record struct) with compiler-generated value-based equality, ToString, deconstruction and non-destructive mutation through `with`.
i: Records are ideal for DTOs, messages and value objects: two ShipmentCreated events with the same data are equal.
Positional records (`record Kit(string Number, int SiteId)`) create init-only properties; `with` makes a copy with changes.
Equality includes the runtime type (EqualityContract), so a derived record never equals its base record.
record struct (C# 10) gives value-type records; readonly record struct makes them immutable.
EF Core entities should usually be classes with identity, not records, because value equality confuses change tracking.
Structs: small, short-lived, immutable values (coordinates, money); large or mutable structs cause copying bugs and costs.
f: Are records immutable?
Positional records have init-only properties, but you can add mutable properties, and referenced objects (lists) can still change.
Why not records for EF entities?
Entities need stable identity and tracked mutation; value equality and with-copies fight that.

p1-14.a: Catch only what you can handle; let the rest bubble to global middleware that logs and returns ProblemDetails.|Use `throw;` not `throw ex;` so the stack trace is kept.|Create domain exceptions (for example StudyTransferNotAllowedException) for business rules, but do not use exceptions for normal flow.|Always log with context (correlation id, study id) and never leak stack traces to clients; use `finally` or `using` for cleanup.
p1-14.qa: Catch exceptions only where you can handle them meaningfully, let the rest bubble to one global handler that logs and returns ProblemDetails, and never swallow them silently. Use specific exception types, preserve stack traces with `throw;`, and do not use exceptions for normal control flow.
i: `throw;` keeps the original stack trace, `throw ex;` resets it; wrap with an inner exception when adding context.
Exception filters (`catch (SqlException ex) when (ex.Number == 1205)`) catch only matching cases without unwinding the stack first, which helps debugging.
Use finally or using/await using for cleanup; IAsyncDisposable for async resources.
Expected outcomes (validation, not found) are often clearer as results or specific domain exceptions mapped to 400/404/409 centrally.
Cancellation: let OperationCanceledException flow when the request is aborted; do not log it as an error.
Logging: log once, at the boundary, with structured context (ids), not at every layer; never expose stack traces to clients.
f: Why not catch (Exception) everywhere?
It hides bugs and leaves state inconsistent; only boundaries (global handler, background loops) should catch everything.
Exceptions vs error codes?
Exceptions for exceptional failures; results for expected business outcomes.

p1-15.a: Generics give type-safe reusable code without boxing (List<T>, Repository<TEntity>).|Constraints (`where T : class, IEntity, new()`) let you call members safely.|Covariance (`out T`, IEnumerable<Derived> as IEnumerable<Base>) and contravariance (`in T`, Action<Base> as Action<Derived>).|Example: a generic Result<T> wrapper for API responses.
p1-15.qa: Generics let you write type-safe, reusable code parameterised by type, such as List<T> or Result<T>, without casting or boxing. Constraints (`where T : class, new(), IEntity`) tell the compiler what T can do, so you can call members on it safely.
i: Performance: generics over value types get specialised code, so List<int> does not box like ArrayList.
Constraints: class, struct, notnull, unmanaged, new(), base class, interface, and in C# 11 static abstract interface members for generic math.
Variance: `out T` (covariance) on IEnumerable<out T> lets IEnumerable<string> be used as IEnumerable<object>; `in T` (contravariance) on Action<in T>.
Generic methods with inference keep call sites clean: `Map<TSource, TDest>()`.
Open generic DI registration: `services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfRepository<>));`.
Used in IRT for [a Result<T> type returned by validation services and a generic paged response PagedResult<T>].
f: What is covariance?
Using a more derived type argument where a less derived one is expected, allowed for out-only positions.
Generics in C# vs Java?
C# generics are reified at runtime (real types per instantiation); Java uses type erasure.

p1-16.a: Big runtime performance gains each release (JIT, GC, dynamic PGO) with almost free speed-ups after upgrade.|Minimal APIs maturing, native AOT for small fast-starting services, built-in rate limiting, keyed DI services (8), better OpenAPI support and System.Text.Json improvements.|Span<T>, Memory<T> and pooling for allocation-free parsing, useful in file and CSV processing.|LTS support windows drive the upgrade plan in a regulated product.
p1-16.qa: For backend services, .NET 8 (LTS) brought big performance gains, native AOT for ASP.NET Core, TimeProvider, keyed DI services, IExceptionHandler, built-in Identity API endpoints, better metrics and the resilience libraries. .NET 10 (LTS, November 2025) adds C# 14, further JIT and GC improvements, built-in minimal API validation, OpenAPI 3.1 and more AOT work.
i: Performance: Dynamic PGO on by default in .NET 8, faster JSON, Kestrel and LINQ; most services get faster just by upgrading.
Native AOT: small, fast-starting binaries for minimal APIs and Lambda; limits on reflection and EF Core.
Developer productivity: primary constructors (C# 12), collection expressions, keyed services, FrozenDictionary, TimeProvider for testable time.
Observability: built-in metrics with System.Diagnostics.Metrics and OpenTelemetry-friendly meters; .NET Aspire for local orchestration and dashboards.
.NET 9 (STS) in between: HybridCache, built-in OpenAPI document generation (Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi), DATAS GC by default.
In IRT we moved from .NET 8 to 10 before .NET 8 support ends (November 2026) and saw [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency.
f: Which C# 14 feature do you like?
Extension members (extension properties and static extension members) and the field keyword for properties.
Why stay on LTS?
Longer support and fewer upgrades, which matters when every upgrade needs validation in a regulated product.

p1-17.a: Each request passes through a chain of middleware components registered in Program.cs; each can act, call `next()`, or short-circuit.|The response flows back through the same chain in reverse.|Order matters: exception handling first, then HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, custom middleware (logging, correlation id), then endpoints.|Custom middleware: a class with `InvokeAsync(HttpContext, RequestDelegate next)`, or inline `app.Use`.
p1-17.qa: The pipeline is the ordered chain of middleware that every HTTP request passes through in ASP.NET Core: Kestrel receives the request, builds an HttpContext, and each middleware can act before and after calling the next one until an endpoint produces the response, which then flows back out in reverse. See Part 10 for standalone deep answers on middleware and custom middleware.
i: Recommended order: exception handler, HSTS, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, custom middleware (rate limiting, correlation id), endpoints.
Routing is split in two: UseRouting selects the endpoint early so later middleware (CORS, auth) can read its metadata; the endpoint executes at the end.
Branching: Map (by path), MapWhen (by predicate, separate branch), UseWhen (conditional middleware that rejoins).
Short-circuit: any middleware can end the request; .NET 8 adds `.ShortCircuit()` on endpoints such as /health to skip the rest of the pipeline.
Cost: every middleware runs for every request, so keep them fast and async.
In IRT the order is exception handler, correlation id, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, controllers.
f: Where does Kestrel fit?
Kestrel is the server underneath; it accepts connections and hands each request to the pipeline.
What does app.Run do at the end of Program.cs?
Starts the host and blocks until shutdown; Run(delegate) in the pipeline is different: a terminal middleware.

p1-18.a: Singleton: one instance for the app lifetime (config, HttpClient factory, caches). Must be thread-safe.|Scoped: one instance per HTTP request (DbContext, unit of work).|Transient: a new instance every time it is resolved (lightweight, stateless helpers).|Captive dependency bug: never inject a Scoped service (like DbContext) into a Singleton; it lives forever and is shared across threads. Use IServiceScopeFactory instead.
p1-18.qa: DI lifetimes define how long a service instance lives: Singleton is one instance for the whole application, Scoped is one per request (per DI scope), Transient is a new instance every time it is resolved. Choose by state and thread safety: stateless or thread-safe shared things as singletons, per-request things like DbContext as scoped, lightweight stateless helpers as transient.
i: Captive dependency: a singleton must not depend on scoped or transient services that hold state, or it keeps them forever; ValidateScopes catches this in Development.
Background code has no request scope: create one with IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope() (or CreateAsyncScope) per unit of work.
Disposal: the container disposes services it created when their scope ends; do not dispose injected services yourself.
Transient IDisposable services resolved from the root provider are kept until app shutdown, a hidden leak.
.NET 8 keyed services let one interface have several named registrations.
In IRT: DbContext scoped, HttpClient typed clients transient via IHttpClientFactory, SFTP provider factory and caches singleton.
f: What is ValidateOnBuild?
It checks at startup that every registered service can be constructed, catching missing registrations early.
Is HttpClient a singleton?
Use IHttpClientFactory or one long-lived client with PooledConnectionLifetime, not new HttpClient per call.

p1-19.a: Controllers: classes with attributes, filters, model binding conventions; good for large APIs with many endpoints.|Minimal APIs: lambdas mapped in Program.cs with less ceremony and slightly better performance; endpoint filters and route groups close most gaps.|Both share the same routing, DI and middleware.|I use controllers in large existing services and minimal APIs for small new microservices or tooling.
p1-19.qa: Controllers group actions in classes with attributes, filters, model binding conventions and [ApiController] behaviour; Minimal APIs map routes directly to lambdas or methods with less ceremony and slightly better performance. Both share routing, DI, auth and OpenAPI, so the choice is about structure and team preference.
i: Controllers: mature conventions, action filters, model validation automatically, great for large APIs and teams used to MVC.
Minimal APIs: route groups, endpoint filters, TypedResults, native AOT support; ideal for small services, Lambda and new code.
Validation: automatic in controllers with [ApiController]; .NET 10 adds built-in validation to minimal APIs (AddValidation).
Testing: both via WebApplicationFactory; minimal handlers can be unit-tested as static methods.
Mixing is fine: one app can have controllers and minimal endpoints.
IRT uses controllers; for [the Node log summariser's .NET replacement prototype] I would use minimal APIs.
f: Which is faster?
Minimal APIs have less overhead, but the difference rarely matters compared with database calls.
How do you organise many minimal endpoints?
MapGroup per feature and one extension method per feature file.

p1-20.a: WebApplication.CreateBuilder sets up configuration (appsettings, environment variables, secrets), logging and the DI container.|You register services (`builder.Services.Add...`), then `Build()`.|You configure the middleware pipeline and map endpoints, then `Run()` starts Kestrel.|Kestrel is the cross-platform web server; in AWS it sits behind a load balancer.
p1-20.qa: Program.cs builds and runs the app with the minimal hosting model: WebApplication.CreateBuilder sets up configuration (appsettings, environment variables, secrets), logging and the DI container; you register services; builder.Build() creates the app; then you configure the middleware pipeline and endpoints; app.Run() starts Kestrel and blocks until shutdown.
i: Configuration sources load in order, later ones override: appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (Development), environment variables, command line.
Services must be registered before Build(); after Build the container is read-only.
Hosted services start before Kestrel starts listening (in registration order); .NET 8 adds IHostedLifecycleService hooks.
Startup validation: ValidateOnStart for options and ValidateOnBuild for DI make misconfiguration fail fast at deployment.
Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM triggers IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping, then hosted services' StopAsync within ShutdownTimeout.
Startup.cs (ConfigureServices/Configure) still works but is no longer the template.
f: Where would you put startup tasks like migrations?
Not in app startup for regulated releases; we run migration scripts as a controlled release step.
What happens if configuration is invalid?
With ValidateOnStart the app fails to start and the health check fails the deployment instead of failing at runtime.

p1-21.a: Middleware is global, runs for every request, and knows only HttpContext.|Filters run inside MVC around actions and know action context: model state, arguments, results.|Filter order: Authorization, Resource, model binding, Action, Exception, Result.|Use middleware for cross-cutting HTTP concerns (logging, correlation id); filters for action-level concerns (validation, audit of a specific action).

steps.title: Authorization filter
steps.detail: Can this user call the action?

steps.title: Action filter
steps.detail: Before and after the action runs

steps.title: Result filter
steps.detail: Before and after the result is written

p1-21.qa: Middleware runs for every request at the HTTP level and knows nothing about MVC; filters run only inside the MVC (or endpoint) pipeline around a selected action, so they can see action arguments, model state and the action result. Use middleware for cross-cutting HTTP concerns and filters for action-specific concerns.
i: Middleware examples: exception handling, correlation id, CORS, authentication, rate limiting, response compression.
Filter examples: validation, auditing an action's arguments, a "study not locked" rule, caching a result, transforming results.
Ordering: middleware order is Program.cs order; filters run authorization, resource, action, exception, result, ordered by scope and Order.
Global exception handling belongs in middleware, because exception filters miss errors from other middleware and result execution.
Minimal APIs use endpoint filters, the filter equivalent.
Detailed filter answer and code: see Part 10 "MVC filter types".
f: Can middleware read the selected endpoint?
Yes, after UseRouting via context.GetEndpoint(), including its metadata (attributes).
Can a filter short-circuit?
Yes, by setting context.Result in an authorization, resource or action filter.

p1-22.a: Model binding maps route, query, header and body data to parameters ([FromRoute], [FromQuery], [FromBody]).|Validation via DataAnnotations or FluentValidation; with [ApiController], invalid models return 400 ProblemDetails automatically.|Validate business rules in the service layer too, not only shape.|For CSV bulk import I validated each row and returned a per-row error report rather than failing the whole file silently.
p1-22.qa: Model binding converts HTTP data (route values, query string, headers, form, JSON body) into action parameters and objects; validation then checks them against rules (DataAnnotations or FluentValidation) and fills ModelState. With [ApiController], invalid models automatically return a 400 ValidationProblemDetails before your action runs.
i: Sources: [FromRoute], [FromQuery], [FromBody] (one per action, read by System.Text.Json input formatter), [FromHeader], [FromForm], [FromServices]; [ApiController] infers most of them.
Complex types from the body are deserialised once; the body stream is not rewindable by default (EnableBuffering if middleware must read it).
Validation attributes: [Required], [Range], [StringLength], [RegularExpression]; IValidatableObject for cross-field rules; FluentValidation for complex rules and better testability.
Over-posting: bind to request DTOs, never directly to EF entities.
Custom binders (IModelBinder) for special formats; TypeConverter or TryParse for simple custom types in minimal APIs.
In IRT request DTOs validate format, while business rules (site active, depot valid) run in the service layer and return 409/422.
f: Why is required validation on a non-nullable value type tricky?
A missing Guid binds to Guid.Empty; use Guid? with [Required] or validate explicitly.
FluentValidation vs DataAnnotations?
FluentValidation keeps rules in testable classes and handles complex conditional rules better.

p1-23.a: Use `UseExceptionHandler` or an IExceptionHandler (.NET 8) / custom middleware at the top of the pipeline.|Map known exceptions to status codes (validation 400, not found 404, conflict 409) and unknown ones to 500.|Return RFC 7807 ProblemDetails with a correlation/trace id; log full detail server-side only.|This keeps controllers clean and responses consistent.
p1-23.qa: Global exception handling catches every unhandled exception in one place, logs it with context, and returns a consistent error response (ProblemDetails) instead of leaking stack traces. In .NET 8 I use UseExceptionHandler with IExceptionHandler implementations and AddProblemDetails; Part 10 has the detailed IExceptionHandler answer with code.
i: Map exception types to status codes centrally: validation 400, not found 404, conflict 409, everything else 500.
Include a traceId or correlation id in the response so users can quote it to support.
Register the handler first in the pipeline; it only catches exceptions from later components.
Development shows the developer exception page; production shows a generic message.
Background services and message consumers need their own try/catch, the HTTP handler does not cover them.
Exceptions after the response has started cannot change the status code; the connection is aborted instead.
f: Why not try/catch in every controller?
Duplication and inconsistency; one handler gives one format and one logging policy.
How do you test it?
Integration test an endpoint that throws and assert the status and ProblemDetails body.

p1-24.a: REST: resources identified by URIs, stateless requests, standard verbs, representations (JSON), cacheability.|GET reads (safe, idempotent); POST creates (not idempotent); PUT replaces (idempotent); PATCH partially updates; DELETE removes (idempotent).|Use proper status codes: 200, 201 with Location, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 500.|For non-idempotent operations that clients may retry, accept an idempotency key.
p1-24.qa: REST models the API as resources identified by URLs, manipulated with standard HTTP methods, stateless requests and representations such as JSON. GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST and PATCH are not (by default).
i: Idempotent means repeating the same request leaves the server in the same state; safe means no state change at all (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS).
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created with Location, 202 Accepted for async jobs, 204 No Content, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 Conflict, 422, 429, 500, 503.
Make POST safe to retry with an Idempotency-Key header stored with the result.
Resource naming: plural nouns (/studies/{id}/sites), no verbs, filtering and paging with query parameters.
HATEOAS and Richardson maturity level 3 are rarely used in practice; consistent conventions and OpenAPI matter more.
Concurrency: ETags with If-Match return 412 on conflicting updates.
f: PUT vs PATCH?
PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH changes some fields (JSON Patch or merge patch).
Is DELETE idempotent if the second call returns 404?
Yes; the state is the same (resource gone), even though the response differs.

p1-25.a: Options: URL segment (/api/v2/...), query string, header, or media type.|I prefer URL segment for clarity, using Asp.Versioning.|Never break existing clients: add fields, do not rename or remove; deprecate with a timeline.|Document each version in OpenAPI/Swagger.
p1-25.qa: API versioning lets you evolve an API without breaking existing clients. Common approaches are URL segment (/api/v2/...), query string (?api-version=2.0), header (api-version or a media type); in ASP.NET Core the Asp.Versioning package handles routing, reporting and deprecation.
i: Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields) so most changes need no new version.
Breaking changes (renamed fields, changed semantics, removed endpoints) get a new major version, with the old one supported for an agreed period.
Report supported and deprecated versions in response headers (api-supported-versions) and announce sunset dates.
Keep versions in OpenAPI documents per version so clients see exactly what they get.
Version message contracts too (events on Kafka) with a schema version field.
In IRT vendor-facing APIs use URL versions because vendors' tools handle them easily.
f: Which approach do you prefer?
URL versioning for external clients (visible, cache-friendly); headers for internal APIs if the team prefers clean URLs.
How long do you keep old versions?
As long as agreed with clients, with usage metrics to see when traffic drops to zero.

p1-26.a: Configuration layers: appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, environment variables, user secrets, then cloud stores (AWS Parameter Store/Secrets Manager).|Bind sections to strongly typed classes with `services.Configure<T>` and inject IOptions<T>, IOptionsSnapshot<T> (per request) or IOptionsMonitor<T> (live changes).|Validate options on start (`ValidateOnStart`).|Never commit secrets.
p1-26.qa: ASP.NET Core configuration merges key-value pairs from providers (appsettings.json, environment-specific files, environment variables, user secrets, command line, Azure App Configuration, AWS Parameter Store) with later sources overriding earlier ones. The Options pattern binds sections to typed classes (IOptions<T>, IOptionsSnapshot<T>, IOptionsMonitor<T>) with validation; Part 10 compares the three in depth.
i: Hierarchical keys use ":" in JSON and "__" in environment variables (Sftp__Vendors__DepotA__Host).
Secrets: user secrets locally, AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store in deployed environments; never commit them.
Validate with ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart so bad config stops the deployment.
Reloading works only with providers that support it (JSON files with reloadOnChange, App Configuration); use IOptionsMonitor to react.
Keep configuration per environment in IaC or variable groups, so environments differ by data, not by code.
f: Why bind to classes instead of IConfiguration["key"]?
Types, validation, IntelliSense and easy testing, with no magic strings scattered around.
How does ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT affect config?
It selects appsettings.{Environment}.json and enables Development-only features such as user secrets.

p1-27.a: Use ILogger<T> with structured logging (message templates, not string concatenation).|Add a correlation id middleware so one request can be traced across microservices and queues.|Ship logs to CloudWatch; build dashboards and alerts in CloudWatch and Grafana.|Log levels: Debug in dev, Information for business events, Warning/Error for problems; never log PHI or secrets, especially in a clinical system.
p1-27.qa: I log with ILogger<T> using structured message templates, enrich every entry with a correlation id through logging scopes, and send JSON logs to a central store (CloudWatch Logs); for tracing I propagate the id (or W3C traceparent) across HTTP and messages so one request can be followed across services. Part 10 covers ILogger and structured logging in depth.
i: Three pillars: logs for details, metrics for trends and alerts, traces for the path and timing of a request across services.
OpenTelemetry in .NET: ActivitySource and Activity give spans; exporters send traces to X-Ray, Jaeger or Tempo; ASP.NET Core and HttpClient are instrumented automatically.
Log levels per category in configuration; avoid Information-level noise from framework namespaces.
Use LoggerMessage source generators on hot paths; never log secrets or patient data.
Metrics: request rate, errors, latency (p95/p99), queue depth; alert on SLOs, not on single errors.
In IRT: correlation-id middleware and a DelegatingHandler, JSON logs to CloudWatch, Grafana dashboards and alarms.
f: Logging vs tracing?
Logs record events; traces connect timed spans of one request across services.
What should every log entry contain?
Timestamp, level, service, environment, version, correlation id and the relevant business ids.

p1-28.a: Measure first: CloudWatch/Grafana metrics, profiling, slow-query logs.|Async I/O end to end; use IHttpClientFactory to avoid socket exhaustion.|Fix the database: indexes, AsNoTracking, projections, pagination, avoiding N+1.|Cache: in-memory or ElastiCache (Redis), output caching; compress responses.|Scale horizontally behind a load balancer once code is efficient.
p1-28.qa: Measure first (Application Insights, CloudWatch, dotnet-counters, a profiler), then fix the biggest bottleneck, which is usually the database: efficient queries, indexes, projections, no N+1. Then use async I/O end to end, caching, response compression, pagination, pooling, and offload long work to background jobs.
i: EF Core: AsNoTracking, Select projections, split queries, compiled queries for hot paths, DbContext pooling.
Avoid sync-over-async and thread-pool starvation; pass CancellationToken.
Caching: output caching or HybridCache for reference data; HTTP caching headers for public data.
Payloads: pagination, smaller DTOs, System.Text.Json source generation, response compression (Brotli/Gzip) where CPU allows.
Platform: upgrading to .NET 8/10 gives free wins (Dynamic PGO); right-size containers and autoscale on latency or CPU.
Prove it: load test with k6 or JMeter before and after; my shipment list fix took [9 seconds to under 300 ms].
f: What is your first step with a slow endpoint?
Find where the time goes: trace spans or logs with durations, then the SQL plan if it is the database.
When does caching hurt?
When data must be consistent (kit allocation) or invalidation is unclear.

p1-29.a: Browsers block cross-origin calls unless the server allows them via CORS headers.|A preflight OPTIONS request checks allowed origin, methods and headers.|In ASP.NET Core: AddCors with a named policy listing exact origins, then UseCors before auth.|Never combine AllowAnyOrigin with credentials.
p1-29.qa: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser mechanism that lets a server say which other origins may call it from JavaScript. The browser sends an Origin header (and a preflight OPTIONS request for non-simple calls), and the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-* headers; in ASP.NET Core you define named policies with AddCors and apply UseCors after UseRouting.
i: CORS is not security for your API: it only restricts browsers; curl, Postman and servers ignore it. Authentication and authorization protect the API.
Preflight happens for methods other than GET/POST/HEAD, custom headers (Authorization) or JSON content type; cache it with SetPreflightMaxAge.
AllowCredentials cannot be combined with AllowAnyOrigin; list exact origins.
Order: UseCors after UseRouting and before UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization so preflights are answered before auth rejects them.
In IRT the API allows only [the IRT UI origins per environment] from configuration.
f: Does CORS stop CSRF?
No; CSRF uses simple requests that may not need preflight. Use SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens.
Why does a preflight fail with 401?
The auth middleware ran before CORS or the OPTIONS request was not allowed; fix the order.

p1-30.a: Timeouts on every call; retries with exponential backoff and jitter only for transient errors and idempotent operations.|Circuit breaker: after repeated failures, stop calling for a while (open), then test with one call (half-open).|Use Polly / Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience with IHttpClientFactory.|Add bulkheads, fallbacks and idempotency keys; for async flows prefer queues.
p1-30.qa: I make service-to-service calls resilient with timeouts on every call, retries with exponential backoff and jitter only for transient failures, circuit breakers to fail fast when a dependency is down, idempotent operations so retries are safe, and fallbacks or asynchronous messaging where an immediate answer is not required. In .NET 8 this is Polly v8 through AddStandardResilienceHandler (Part 10 has the deep answer).
i: Timeouts: without them a slow dependency ties up threads and connections; set per-attempt and total timeouts.
Transient = timeouts, 5xx, 408, 429, connection resets; respect Retry-After.
Circuit breaker states: closed, open (fail fast), half-open (trial calls).
Bulkheads and concurrency limits isolate one slow dependency.
Idempotency keys make POST retries safe; consumers dedupe messages by id.
Observe it: metrics on retries and breaker state, alerts when a breaker opens.
f: What is a retry storm?
Many clients retrying aggressively at once, multiplying load on a struggling service; backoff, jitter and breakers prevent it.
Sync call or message?
If the caller does not need the answer now, publish a message and let the consumer retry independently.

p1-31.a: REST: resource-based over HTTP/JSON; simple, cacheable, universal.|SOAP/WCF: XML envelopes, strict contracts (WSDL), WS-* security; common in older enterprise systems.|gRPC: binary Protobuf over HTTP/2, fast, streaming; good for internal service-to-service.|GraphQL: clients ask for exactly the fields they need from one endpoint; good for varied front ends.
p1-31.qa: REST uses HTTP resources and JSON, simple and universal; SOAP (WCF) uses XML envelopes and a strict WSDL contract with WS-* standards; gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for fast, strongly typed service-to-service calls and streaming; GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need from one endpoint.
i: REST: best for public and browser APIs, caching, broad tooling; risk of over- or under-fetching.
SOAP: legacy enterprise integrations, WS-Security, transactions; heavy and verbose; CoreWCF helps migrate.
gRPC: binary, compact, contract-first .proto, bidirectional streaming, deadlines; limited browser support (gRPC-Web), harder to debug by hand.
GraphQL: flexible queries for many front ends, one round trip; needs care with N+1 resolvers (DataLoader), caching and query cost limits.
In IRT: REST for UI and vendors, legacy WCF endpoints in older areas, Kafka and RabbitMQ for async.
f: When would you pick gRPC?
Internal high-throughput service calls or streaming between services you control.
Why not GraphQL everywhere?
Extra complexity in caching, security and performance control that simple REST APIs do not need.

p1-32.a: Implement BackgroundService (IHostedService) for long-running loops such as queue consumers.|Create a scope inside for scoped services like DbContext.|Honour the stopping token for graceful shutdown.|For heavy or scheduled work, prefer a separate worker service, Lambda or a queue rather than doing it inside a web request.
p1-32.qa: Short background work uses hosted services (BackgroundService) with queues such as Channels; durable or scheduled work uses a message broker (RabbitMQ, SQS) or a scheduler (Hangfire, Quartz); long-running or heavy jobs run in separate worker services or Lambda. Never use fire-and-forget Task.Run inside a request. Part 10 covers BackgroundService in depth.
i: Request returns 202 Accepted with a job id, a worker processes it, and the client polls or gets notified.
Hosted services are singletons; create scopes for DbContext.
Graceful shutdown: honour the stopping token and finish or checkpoint work within the shutdown timeout.
Multiple instances run every hosted service; avoid duplicate work with queues or distributed locks.
In IRT: RabbitMQ consumers as BackgroundServices in worker containers, [an SFTP poller], and Ansible-driven deployment jobs outside the app.
f: Why not Task.Run in a controller?
The work is lost on shutdown or crash, exceptions vanish, and it has no retries or visibility.
Hangfire vs hosted service?
Hangfire adds persistence, retries, cron and a dashboard; a hosted service is a simple in-process loop.

p1-33.a: The DbContext tracks loaded entities and their state: Added, Unchanged, Modified, Deleted, Detached.|SaveChanges compares snapshots and generates INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in one transaction.|AsNoTracking skips tracking for read-only queries: faster and less memory, ideal for GET endpoints and reports.|For bulk updates use ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete (EF Core 7+) instead of loading rows.
p1-33.qa: EF Core's change tracker keeps a snapshot of every entity it loads; on SaveChanges it compares current values with the snapshot (DetectChanges) and generates INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements for what changed. AsNoTracking skips the snapshot and identity resolution, so read-only queries are faster and use less memory.
i: Entity states: Detached, Added, Unchanged, Modified, Deleted; inspect with context.Entry(e).State or ChangeTracker.DebugView.
Identity resolution: a tracked context returns the same instance for the same key; AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution keeps that without tracking.
Updates only include changed columns, which reduces conflicts and log noise.
Long-lived contexts accumulate tracked entities and slow down; keep DbContext short-lived (per request).
Disconnected updates: attach and set state, or load then apply changes; for bulk changes use ExecuteUpdate which bypasses tracking entirely.
In IRT all GET endpoints use AsNoTracking with projections; writes load, modify and save.
f: Is tracking needed to update?
Not strictly; you can Attach and mark properties modified, or use ExecuteUpdate for set-based changes.
Can you make no-tracking the default?
Yes, UseQueryTrackingBehavior(QueryTrackingBehavior.NoTracking) on the context options.

p1-34.a: Eager: `Include` loads related data in the same query.|Lazy: related data loads on first access (proxies); convenient but causes N+1 queries.|Explicit: you call `Entry(x).Collection(...).Load()` when needed.|N+1: one query for parents plus one per child. Fix with Include, projections (`Select` into DTOs) or split queries.

rows: You know you need the children

p1-34.qa: Eager loading fetches related data in the same query with Include/ThenInclude; lazy loading fetches it automatically when you first access the navigation (needs proxies or ILazyLoader); explicit loading fetches it on demand with Entry(e).Collection(...).LoadAsync(). The N+1 problem is one query for the parents plus one more query per parent for its children, which is what lazy loading in a loop produces.
i: Detect N+1 by logging SQL or watching query counts in tests; it often hides behind serialisation of navigations.
Fix with Include, or better, a Select projection that pulls exactly the needed columns in one query.
Large Includes cause cartesian explosion; AsSplitQuery runs one query per collection instead.
Lazy loading is off by default in EF Core and I keep it off in APIs because it hides database calls.
Filtered Include (EF Core 5+): Include(s => s.Shipments.Where(x => x.Status == "Open")).
c:
var sites = await _db.Sites.AsNoTracking()
    .Where(s => s.StudyId == studyId)
    .Select(s => new { s.Name, Open = s.Shipments.Count(x => x.Status == "Open") })
    .ToListAsync(ct);   // one query, no N+1
f: Split query vs single query?
Split avoids duplicated rows for multiple collections but runs several round trips and can see inconsistent data without a transaction.
Why not lazy loading in APIs?
It triggers unpredictable queries, often during JSON serialisation, after the context may be disposed.

p1-35.a: Generate migrations in code, but deploy idempotent SQL scripts (`dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent`) that are reviewed.|Apply them through the release pipeline per environment (FV, TechOps, UAT, production), not automatically at app start.|Keep migrations backward compatible so old and new app versions can run during a rollout (expand, then contract).|Version scripts with the release tag for traceability.
p1-35.qa: Migrations are code-reviewed like any change, generated as idempotent SQL scripts (dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent), and applied as a controlled step of the release through FV, UAT and production, never by the app at startup. Scripts are versioned with the release, backward compatible with the previous app version, and kept as evidence.
i: Expand/contract: add new columns or tables first (nullable or with defaults), deploy the app, backfill, then remove old ones in a later release; this allows rollback of the app without database rollback.
Review generated Up code for destructive operations (drops, renames that EF sees as drop and add) and data loss.
Large tables: add indexes ONLINE where the edition allows and batch data migrations to avoid long locks.
Migration bundles (efbundle) are an alternative executable for pipelines.
Keep a __EFMigrationsHistory check in verification so every environment is on the expected migration.
In IRT DB scripts are deployed first in the release order (DB, API, app, UI) by the Ansible/Shell install scripts.
c:
dotnet ef migrations add AddShipmentStatusIndex
dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent -o release/2024.3/db.sql
f: Why not context.Database.Migrate() at startup?
Several instances could race, it needs elevated DB rights, and regulated releases need a reviewed, controlled script.
How do you roll back a migration?
Prefer forward fixes; with expand/contract the old app still works, so the DB rarely needs rolling back.

p1-36.a: Optimistic concurrency: add a rowversion/timestamp column marked as a concurrency token.|EF adds it to the WHERE clause; if no row is updated it throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException.|Resolve by reloading and retrying, merging, or returning 409 Conflict to the user.|Pessimistic locking (UPDLOCK) only for short, critical sections such as allocating limited drug supply.
p1-36.qa: EF Core uses optimistic concurrency: mark a concurrency token (a SQL Server rowversion column with [Timestamp] or IsRowVersion), EF adds it to the WHERE clause of updates, and if no row is affected it throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. You then decide: reload and retry, merge, or return 409 Conflict to the user.
i: rowversion changes automatically on every update, so it is the simplest token in SQL Server.
In APIs return the version as an ETag; clients send If-Match, and a mismatch becomes 412 or 409.
Handling: ex.Entries gives current, original and database values for merging or messages.
Pessimistic alternative: UPDLOCK/transactions for high-contention rows (allocating the last kit), used sparingly.
Bulk ExecuteUpdate bypasses the token unless you include it in the Where.
f: Optimistic vs pessimistic?
Optimistic for low contention and web apps (no held locks); pessimistic only for short, high-contention critical sections.
Where else do you use it?
Study configuration edits by several study managers, where silent overwrites would be a GxP data-integrity problem.

p1-37.a: DbContext is a unit of work, registered as Scoped (one per request).|It is not thread-safe: never share it across parallel tasks.|In background services create a scope per unit of work.|AddDbContextPool reuses instances for performance in high-throughput APIs.
p1-37.qa: DbContext is a lightweight unit of work that is not thread-safe, so it should be short-lived: one per request (scoped, the AddDbContext default) or one per unit of work in background services. Never share one instance across concurrent operations; running two queries in parallel on the same context throws InvalidOperationException.
i: Parallel work: create separate contexts with IDbContextFactory<T> (AddDbContextFactory) per task.
Pooling: AddDbContextPool reuses context instances to reduce allocation cost; the context must not hold per-request state in fields.
Singletons and hosted services must not capture a scoped DbContext; create a scope or use the factory.
Long-lived contexts grow their change tracker and give stale data.
Connection pooling is separate and handled by SqlClient; the context opens and closes connections per operation.
f: What error do you get when sharing a context concurrently?
"A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed."
Pool vs factory?
Pooling reduces cost for scoped contexts; the factory gives you control over when to create contexts (and can also be pooled).

p1-38.a: Use FromSql / FromSqlInterpolated or ExecuteSqlInterpolated; interpolated values become parameters.|Never build SQL by string concatenation with user input (SQL injection).|Map results to entities or keyless types.|Use raw SQL for tuned queries the LINQ provider cannot express efficiently.
p1-38.qa: Use FromSql / FromSqlInterpolated or SqlQuery with interpolated strings, which EF converts into parameters, or explicit SqlParameter objects; never concatenate user input into SQL. For commands use ExecuteSql/ExecuteSqlInterpolated, and for stored procedures `FromSql($"EXEC dbo.GetSiteStock {siteId}")`.
i: FromSqlRaw with string concatenation is the classic SQL injection hole; FromSqlRaw is fine only with placeholders and parameters.
FromSql results can be composed with LINQ (EF wraps it as a subquery) if the SQL is composable (not a stored procedure).
SqlQuery<T> (EF Core 8) maps raw SQL to unmapped types such as DTOs.
Use raw SQL for complex reporting, window functions or hints that LINQ cannot express well; keep it in one place and test it.
Least privilege: the app's DB user cannot alter schema in production.
c:
var stock = await _db.Database
    .SqlQuery<KitStock>($"EXEC dbo.GetSiteStock @SiteId = {siteId}")
    .ToListAsync(ct);   // {siteId} becomes a SqlParameter, not string concatenation
f: Is FromSqlInterpolated safe?
Yes, interpolated values become parameters; the danger is building the string first and passing it to FromSqlRaw.
Dapper or EF raw SQL?
Dapper for many hand-written queries and maximum speed; EF raw SQL when you are already in an EF context.

p1-39.a: A single SaveChanges is atomic by default.|For several SaveChanges or mixed raw SQL, use `Database.BeginTransaction()` and commit/rollback.|Across services you cannot use one DB transaction; use the outbox pattern or a saga.|Keep transactions short to reduce locking and deadlocks.
p1-39.qa: SaveChanges runs all pending changes in one transaction automatically. For several SaveChanges calls or mixing EF with raw SQL, start an explicit transaction with Database.BeginTransactionAsync and commit at the end; across databases or systems use the outbox pattern rather than distributed transactions.
i: Execution strategies (EnableRetryOnFailure) retry transient failures, but with explicit transactions you must wrap the whole block in strategy.ExecuteAsync.
Savepoints: EF Core creates them automatically when SaveChanges runs inside a user transaction, so a failed SaveChanges can roll back to the savepoint.
TransactionScope works but async needs TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled, and it can escalate to distributed transactions; I prefer explicit DbContext transactions.
Isolation level can be passed to BeginTransaction; defaults to the database default (READ COMMITTED, or snapshot if enabled).
In the CSV import all batches run inside one transaction so a failure rolls back everything.
f: What is the outbox pattern?
Save the business change and the outgoing message in the same DB transaction, then a relay publishes it, so you never lose or invent events.
Why not distributed transactions (MSDTC)?
Slow, fragile and unsupported in many cloud setups; sagas and outbox are the modern approach.

p1-40.a: WCF (Windows Communication Foundation) is the .NET Framework technology for SOAP and other service communication.|A = Address (where), B = Binding (how: basicHttpBinding, wsHttpBinding, netTcpBinding), C = Contract (what: ServiceContract, OperationContract, DataContract).|It supports WS-Security, transactions and reliable messaging.|In IRT some older services expose WCF endpoints alongside newer REST APIs.
p1-40.qa: WCF (Windows Communication Foundation) is the .NET Framework framework for building service-oriented applications over SOAP and other transports. Every endpoint has ABC: Address (where), Binding (how: transport, encoding, security, such as basicHttpBinding or netTcpBinding) and Contract (what: the [ServiceContract] interface).
i: Bindings choose protocol and features: BasicHttpBinding (SOAP 1.1, interop), WSHttpBinding (WS-Security, reliable sessions), NetTcpBinding (fast .NET to .NET), NetNamedPipeBinding (same machine).
Contracts: ServiceContract, OperationContract, DataContract/DataMember, FaultContract for typed errors.
Behaviours configure throttling, instance mode (PerCall, PerSession, Single) and concurrency.
Hosting: IIS/WAS, Windows service or self-host; heavy XML configuration in web.config.
Modern status: no WCF server in .NET 5+, CoreWCF provides a community port; clients still work via System.ServiceModel packages.
In IRT older areas still expose WCF endpoints that we maintain and integrate with.
f: What is a FaultContract?
A typed SOAP fault the service declares so clients can handle specific errors.
PerCall vs PerSession?
PerCall creates a service instance per request (scalable); PerSession keeps one per client session (stateful).

p1-41.a: Option 1: CoreWCF, a community port that keeps SOAP contracts so existing clients do not change.|Option 2: re-expose as REST (ASP.NET Core) or gRPC and add an adapter for old clients during transition.|Move business logic into shared libraries first so the transport becomes a thin layer.|Migrate endpoint by endpoint (strangler fig), with contract tests to prove identical behaviour.
p1-41.qa: I would migrate WCF gradually: inventory endpoints and clients, keep the contracts stable, then either port to CoreWCF on modern .NET when SOAP clients cannot change, or move to REST (ASP.NET Core) or gRPC when clients can. Run old and new side by side behind a facade, compare responses, and cut clients over one by one.
i: Strangler fig pattern: route endpoint by endpoint to the new implementation while the old service keeps running.
Shared business logic moves into .NET Standard or modern libraries first, so both hosts use the same code.
WS-* features (message security, transactions, reliable sessions) need replacements: TLS and OAuth, outbox/sagas, idempotent retries.
Contract tests that replay recorded requests against old and new services prove compatibility.
Plan for configuration (no web.config), hosting (Kestrel, containers) and authentication changes.
f: CoreWCF or gRPC?
CoreWCF when external SOAP clients cannot change; gRPC for internal .NET-to-.NET calls you control.
Biggest risk?
Hidden behaviour in bindings and serializers (DataContract quirks, faults) that clients depend on.

A GxP product has to stay on a supported runtime, so we planned the move to .NET 10 LTS.|Task: I owned the upgrade of [3] of those services end to end, with no change in behaviour, inside [one release cycle].|Action: I listed every project, NuGet package and Docker base image and upgraded the shared libraries first, because every service used them. Then I changed TargetFramework to net10.0, updated the SDK on the build agents, the Dockerfiles and the pipeline YAML, and updated packages such as EF Core and the test libraries. I fixed the obsolete-API and analyzer warnings listed in the breaking-change notes, and ran unit, integration and Playwright tests. On the validation environment I compared response times and memory before and after.|Result: all [3] services went through FV, TechOps, UAT and production with [no functional defects]. We measured about [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency and [about 10 percent] lower memory, which matches the runtime improvements Microsoft publishes.
